title: 道德經 第七十一章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 71, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 88. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 71 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 知病 (Knowing the Sickness). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
知不知上，
不知知病。

morph.gloss: to know — with 不 in front of it this pair is the OBJECT of the first 知: the not-knowing that is known
the top, the highest — the adjective standing alone as the whole predicate
to know, knowing — the object of the 不知 before it; what that object amounts to is the crux, see the note
a sickness, an ailment; and so the flaw, the thing that does the damage

sentences.l:
Knowing not-knowing: highest;
not-knowing knowing: a sickness.
sentences.i: To know that you do not know is highest; not to know, and to rely on knowing all the same, is a sickness.
sentences.n:
Eight characters, four of them the same character, and no verb 'to be' anywhere: 上 and 病 are simply set down after their subjects and that is the whole predication. The two halves are a mirror — 知不知 against 不知知 — and Chinese can build that shape because 知 needs no ending to change from the verb 'know' to the thing known.

The second half is elliptical in a way English cannot copy. 不知知 says only 'not-know know', and what stands between the two has to be supplied by the reader. Wang Bi supplies it one way: his comment runs 不知知之不足任，則病也 — 'not to know that knowing is not enough to be relied on: that is the sickness' — taking the object of 不知 to be a whole clause. Most later readers supply it the other way: the man does not know, and takes himself to know regardless. The English here is worded to carry both, because the Chinese does not choose between them.

The Mawangdui silk manuscripts are reported to read 尚 'esteemed' for 上, and to double the 不知 in the second half (不知不知), which would give 'not to know that one does not know'. Whether that is an older reading or a copyist's slip is not settled; the received text is what is printed here.

sentences.t:
夫唯病病，
是以不病。
聖人不病，
以其病病，
是以不病。

morph.gloss: now, as for —— (the sentence-opening particle, read fú; read fū it is the noun 'a grown man')
to count as a sickness, to reckon it an ailment — the noun now working as a verb
therefore, and so — a fused connective; neither half gives you it alone
the sage — in this book the ruler who holds the Way, not a moral saint
because of, by reason of — 以 in its causal job, not the usual 'by means of'
therefore, and so — a fused connective; neither half gives you it alone

sentences.l:
Now, it is only counting sickness a sickness —
therefore not sick.
The sage is not sick:
by his counting sickness a sickness,
therefore not sick.
sentences.i: It is only by taking the sickness for a sickness that one is free of it. The sage is not sick, because he takes the sickness for a sickness — and so he is not sick.
sentences.n:
病病 is the putative construction you met in chapter 63's 猶難之, 'still treats it as difficult': a word for a quality, used as a verb, means 'to reckon something that quality'. So the first 病 is 'to count as a sickness' and the second is the sickness counted. Nothing in the writing distinguishes them; only the position does.

Count the jobs 病 does in these five lines — verb 'reckon a sickness', noun 'the sickness', verb 'be sick', and then all three again. Six occurrences of one character, no inflection at any point. This is Classical Chinese working at full stretch, and it is why the notes in this book do more work than a translation's usually would.

夫唯 X 是以 Y is the clinching frame: 'it is precisely because X that Y'. 夫唯 opens the same move nine times before this chapter — usually with 故 for the second half (chapter 22's 夫唯不爭，故天下莫能與之爭) and with 是以 in chapter 2 and chapter 70's 夫唯無知，是以不我知. And 以其 in the fourth line is the same 以 you know as 'by means of', turned to cause: 'because his ——'.

The argument is small and closed. The sickness is thinking you know; there is no cure that consists of knowing more, since more knowing is the disease. What is left is to see the thing as a sickness — which is the one piece of knowledge that does not make it worse.
